This is just a discussion thread - there will be an upcoming motion with some amendments, but I wanted to get thoughts and feedback from the community first.

I'd like to add some core values to the constitution - basically statements representing how the sub will be run in principle. The following were what I came up with:

  • Moderators will be servant leaders.
  • Moderators will uphold free speech wherever possible.
  • Moderators will allow the community to control content wherever possible.
  • Moderators will seek community feedback on topical issues whenever necessary.

Do people agree/disagree with these? Does anyone thing other statements should be added to this? Does anyone think the statements could be better worded, etc?
Looking for feedback on core values...

@thegoldenboy @Scandinavian @Mick @kneegrow @G4

What are your thoughts?

Moderators will allow the community to control content wherever possible

I think this is a good point to make. If we want to avoid the mistakes of the past (Reddit) moderators should have the smallest influence possible. It is only when we have exceptions such as illegal content and spammers that moderators should step in.

These values are pretty good and I agree with all of them. But I don't see the point. This is a voluntary position, we moderate because we care about the subverse. Right now, if a mod is breaking the moderation rules (allowing spam, censoring content etc) they can get demodded by you. When @system takes over, there's literally nothing that will stop any mod from doing whatever the fuck they want. There are no guarantees.

If we pledge to this and someone breaks the pledge, what's gonna happen? They'll get fired? Downvoted? It's a position that, again, is voluntary. Taking a shit on the community is not in anyone's best interest. My english is horrible so I'll explain by giving an example:

Taking a shit on your subverse is the equivalent of running your company to the ground intentionally. It's still your company, and you just shat in your own hands.

Now, I'm not saying this to target other mods. We have a great mod team and I love every single one of you guys and I know you won't do this kind of shit with @system as head. This is mostly to those who are worried about the future of the sub after @reow's gone. You can either be very worried since there's no legal document that forces us to follow these rules, or you can chill because that won't happen since it's not in anyone's best interest to ruin the sub.

Just to be clear, the issue of these values being added is separate to the pledge. I'll address these values first, and the pledge/consequences second.

Regarding these values... My hope is to provide some broad guidelines, not specific rules. In a sense, they are reassurances to the community on how the sub will be run. At present the constitution and bylaws are a single document, which is 99% bylaws; I'd like to split that. The constitution should be high-level. It should be the governing principles of the sub, nothing more. Effectively the things we all believe in and stand for. The only reason I put "moderators" in each of those statements is because I don't want to impose additional rules on the community, and I don't want the statements being misinterpreted as though regular users have some particular onus.

Regarding the pledge... No current mod is going to be forced to make it - they have to choose to. The pledge in and of itself (as you rightly surmised) offers no guarantee - any mod can violate their word, but who wants to be known as an oath breaker? If any mod starts deliberately abusing their power after the move to @system, a vote will be called for. If the verdict in unanimous amongst the other mods the violating mod will be stood down (§5.3.2). The admins are aware that we operate under a constitution - if the vote passes and they are sent a copy of the thread, I am certain they will demod the person. Let's hope it never comes to that.

Again, while I have no problem with the constitution or the new values.. I don't see the point of it all. If you go to the constitution thread I encourage you to look at two things: the score and the top comments. The post itself is controversial and the top comment, I believe @GOT said it best: Moderators need to stop making meta posts and learn to keep quiet and continue their low-key unimportant roles and stop trying to complicate things. The only thing I think is worth saving is The Governing Council, as it's a pretty cool idea. But it should move to /v/AskVoatMeta.

We're all here to have a good time and enjoy some questions and answers. There's no need for any of this.

If Everyone Gets Electricity, Can the Planet Survive?

I've seen a lot about liquid thorium reactors. I'm no Nuclear Engineer, but it seems like a pretty decent technology and I haven't been able to figure out why we're not putting more effort into it other than people are afraid of the word "nuclear".

Also, the idea of off grid solutions sounds a lot better to me than keeping with the grid model. It requires a lot of resources to build a grid, keep it maintained and plan for upgrades as usage increases. Not to mention when natural disasters happen and people can be out for weeks or months. Or even if its just a particularly hot day and one overload triggered outage causes a domino effect across large sections of a continent. The goal should be with clean power generation and storage at the home or near the home. Most commercial buildings have backup generators, and its becoming popular with homeowners. With solar panels, natural gas (or propane) backup generator, small wind turbines and Tesla's Powerwall you could say bye bye to the grid. Or at least, work with much smaller and easier to manage neighborhood or block level grids.
